label: Atlantic
rationale: Oh Yeah is the one Mingus album on which he leads from the piano instead of the bass, and it is a defining statement of his composing voice — blues, gospel, sardonic song and group shout all built around his own playing and singing [S1,S3] (obs). Recorded at Atlantic Studios, New York City, on November 6, 1961, produced by Nesuhi Ertegün and engineered by Tom Dowd and Phil Iehle [S1,S2] (obs). Session gravity is exceptional: five of Mingus's working band — Dannie Richmond, Doug Watkins, Jimmy Knepper, Booker Ervin — with Rahsaan Roland Kirk, still credited as 'Roland Kirk', doubling on tenor saxophone, flute, manzello, stritch and siren, one of Kirk's earliest appearances on a major-label jazz date [S1,S2,S3] (obs). Consensus: AllMusic rates it 5 of 5 and files it Post-Bop / Avant-Garde Jazz, with Steve Huey's review treating it as a Mingus essential; DownBeat's 1962 review gave 3 1/2 of 5 and the Penguin Guide to Jazz 3 of 5 [S1,S3] (obs). Lineage: the disc sits on the same 1959-63 Atlantic spine as Mingus Ah Um, Blues & Roots and The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady, all already in the canon, and carries the blues-and-gospel hard-bop language forward while opening the door to the avant-garde Mingus would embrace next [S1,S3] (inf). It still plays: 'Hog Callin' Blues', 'Eat That Chicken' and 'Oh Lord, Don't Let Them Drop That Atomic Bomb on Me' are among the most immediately enjoyable records in his catalogue [S1] (obs). Priority is strong rather than must_have: the canon already holds four Mingus albums, and this is the pianist chapter it does not yet have.

personnel.name: Charles Mingus
personnel.notes: Plays piano rather than his usual double bass throughout — the only Mingus album led from the keyboard — and sings on three tracks; sources do not enumerate which three. Also credited as composer and lyricist of all titles.

personnel.name: Rahsaan Roland Kirk
personnel.notes: Credited as 'Roland Kirk' on the original release. Also plays flute, manzello, stritch and siren (jazzdisco; Wikipedia); manzello and stritch are Kirk's modified saxophone relatives and have no taxonomy entry, so the primary horn is recorded as tenor saxophone.

personnel.name: Booker Ervin
personnel.notes: Mingus's tenor of the period (The Freedom Book, already in the canon, is Ervin's own).

personnel.name: Doug Watkins
personnel.notes: Credited simply as 'bass' in sources; takes over the bass chair while Mingus plays piano.

tracks.title: Oh Lord Don't Let Them Drop That Atomic Bomb on Me

personnel_record.notes: Single session: November 6, 1961, Atlantic Studios, New York City (jazzdisco matrix numbers 5756-5768; the album is Atlantic LP 1377 / SD 1377). Seven tracks made the original April 1962 LP (44:08 total); tracks 8-10 here are the three additional numbers cut at the same session and released later (on Tonight at Noon, 1964, and on the 1999 Rhino CD), flagged as bonus tracks. Per-track personnel coverage is not documented by the sources — they list the album's personnel for the one session — so the per-track arrays repeat the documented sextet with epistemic_track 'inf' and track_assignments_complete is false. Epistemic note on conflicts: AllMusic's credit list also carries four names tagged only 'Musician' — Chris Clarke, Faye Rosen, Ginger Spangler and Mark Pinkus — which do not appear in Wikipedia's or jazzdisco's personnel and correspond to no documented performer on this date (they appear to be reissue/compilation metadata); they are recorded here as a conflict and not entered as performers. AllMusic spells the engineer 'Phil Lehle'; Wikipedia gives 'Phil Iehle' — the latter is used, with the variant noted. Wikipedia's bonus-track durations (7:58 / 9:49 / 4:48) differ slightly from AllMusic's (8:59 / 9:48 / 4:55); Wikipedia's are used. Original LP side split is not documented by the sources consulted, so side is left null.

ballot.case_for: This is a singular chapter in Mingus’s work: he leads from piano and sings, bringing blues, gospel, humor, and political bite to a distinctive set of originals (S1, S3). The session pairs his working band—including Booker Ervin, Jimmy Knepper, and Dannie Richmond—with Rahsaan Roland Kirk in an early major-label appearance, giving the date substantial session gravity (S1, S2). Its immediate, earthy performances and place alongside Mingus’s Atlantic-era statements make it a strong discovery record; AllMusic rates it 5/5 and treats it as an essential Mingus album (S1, S3).
ballot.case_against: The critical-consensus case is mixed: the dossier reports a 3/5 from the Penguin Guide and 3.5/5 from DownBeat, below the standing of Mingus’s most widely recognized landmark albums (S1). Its piano-led format is distinctive, but that distinctiveness may make it an illuminating variation rather than a defining compositional statement, and it lacks the bass-driven ensemble force central to Mingus’s signature sound. The dossier also notes incomplete per-track personnel assignments, though that limits track-level certainty more than it undermines the album’s overall case.
ballot.recommendation: John should consider adding it as a strong, contested entry that fills out Mingus’s musical range without treating it as an unquestioned pillar.
